clue.text: Composer may cause havoc to Sikhs?

indicators.note: the letters that follow may be caused to form something new, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether some composer's music might wreak destruction among a Sikh community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'havoc' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder: the letters of HAVOC TO SIKHS, shaken up because they 'may cause' something, make the Russian composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dmitri Shostakovich was a twentieth-century Russian composer of symphonies and string quartets.

clue.text: Where O'Hara proposed a date in 1934

definitions.text: Where O'Hara proposed a date in 1934

parts.words: Where O'Hara proposed a date in 1934
parts.note: John O'Hara's 1934 novel title speaks of an appointment, a date, in a certain Iraqi city

explanation.surface: A man named O'Hara arranges a romantic outing somewhere back in 1934.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'date' is an appointment: John O'Hara's first novel, 1934, is Appointment in Samarra, named from the old story of Death keeping an appointment there.
explanation.definitionFit: Appointment in Samarra is John O'Hara's 1934 novel, the city its title names.

clue.text: Philosopher specializing in close shaves?

parts.note: a medieval thinker famous for his razor, the principle of cutting away needless assumptions

explanation.surface: A thinker who is an expert barber, or one who often narrowly escapes danger.
explanation.walkthrough: William of Ockham's razor says entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity, so he 'shaves' theories closely.
explanation.definitionFit: William of Occam, an English friar and logician, gave his name to the principle called Occam's razor.

clue.text: A chart key may indicate novelist

indicators.note: the clue's letters may point to the name once reordered, so they are to be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The legend on a map or graph might point to some writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may indicate' is the anagram signal here: the letters of A CHART KEY rearrange to the Victorian novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: William Makepeace Thackeray was the Victorian author of Vanity Fair.

clue.text: Sort of yard school of J. M. Barrie and Ian Maclaren

definitions.text: Sort of yard school of J. M. Barrie and Ian Maclaren

parts.words: Sort of yard school of J. M. Barrie and Ian Maclaren
parts.note: these Scottish writers were grouped as a school named after a cabbage patch

explanation.surface: A kind of playground school once attended by two Scottish writers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Kailyard school' was a label for sentimental Scottish rural fiction by Barrie and Maclaren; a kailyard is a cabbage garden, kail being Scots for kale.
explanation.definitionFit: Kail is the Scots spelling of kale, the cabbage of the kailyard that named Barrie and Maclaren's school.

clue.text: Underwear intended, say, for ceremonial use

parts.note: a vest is an undershirt in British usage

indicators.note: say signals that the following word is to be heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: intended means meant

explanation.surface: Undergarments purposely designed to be worn at formal rites.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a vest is an undershirt. 'say' turns MEANT into its sound-alike MENT; the definition is descriptive, a garment 'for ceremonial use'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vestment is a robe worn by clergy during services, a garment kept for liturgy.

clue.text: Loaded weapons from Italy in police stick collection

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the letters of the words police stick

explanation.surface: Weapons from Italy found among a collection of truncheons.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is found spanning 'police' and 'stick'. Cesti (singular cestus) were ancient Roman boxing gloves weighted with lead or iron.
explanation.definitionFit: The cestus was a Roman boxer's glove weighted with metal, hence a loaded weapon from Italy.

clue.text: Music all derived from Livy's "second founder of Rome"

indicators.note: derived suggests the letters are drawn out and rearranged into a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Every piece of music taken from the Roman historian's account of a hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'derived' is the anagram signal on MUSIC ALL. Marcus Furius Camillus, who drove out the Gauls, is called Rome's second founder by Livy.
explanation.definitionFit: Livy credits the general Marcus Furius Camillus with refounding the city after the Gallic sack.

clue.text: O'Neill's Christie in extremely heavy Buchan role

indicators.note: in places one piece within the first and last letters of heavy
extremely asks for the extreme letters, the first and last, of the word heavy

parts.note: Eugene O'Neill's play is Anna Christie, its heroine Anna

explanation.surface: A Eugene O'Neill heroine is cast in a very weighty part in a John Buchan story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely heavy' gives the first and last letters H and Y; ANNA (O'Neill's Anna Christie) goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Hannay is the hero of John Buchan's The Thirty-Nine Steps and its sequels.

clue.text: "Dismiss my soldiers, or capitulate / Again with Rome's" (Coriolanus)

definitions.text: "Dismiss my soldiers, or capitulate / Again with Rome's" (Coriolanus)

parts.words: Dismiss my soldiers, or capitulate / Again with Rome's
parts.note: Coriolanus refuses to come to terms with the working men of Rome; the missing word ends the quotation

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Coriolanus with its final word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap: Coriolanus scorns 'Rome's mechanics', the old word for manual workers and tradesmen.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's day mechanics meant artisans, the labouring common people of Rome.

clue.text: State in South America gets opera house

indicators.note: in places the state's abbreviation within the letters for South and America

parts.note: Cal is a short form for California

explanation.surface: A country in South America acquires a grand theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South America' is split: S and A, with CAL (California) inside.
explanation.definitionFit: La Scala in Milan is Italy's most famous theatre for opera.

clue.text: New version of Christine Brooke-Rose

definitions.meaning: a film or work made over again
her 1996 autobiographical novel bears this title

explanation.surface: An updated edition of a book by Christine Brooke-Rose.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresh rendering of an old film is so called, and Brooke-Rose used the same word as a novel title.

clue.text: Aim to bin new version of W. H. Davies work

indicators.note: a new version of the words means the letters are reorganised

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A plan to discard a fresh edition of a Welsh poet's writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new version of' is the anagram signal on AIM TO BIN; 'Aim' looks like the definition but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambition is a poem by the Welsh poet W. H. Davies, author of Leisure.

clue.text: Resource available to casting director of Hitchcock version of Du Maurier story

definitions.text: Resource available to casting director of Hitchcock version of Du Maurier story

parts.words: Resource available to casting director of Hitchcock version of Du Maurier story
parts.note: Hitchcock filmed Daphne du Maurier's The Birds, so whoever cast it needed a supply of feathered performers

explanation.surface: What a Hollywood casting director might draw on for a Hitchcock thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: Hitchcock's The Birds came from Daphne du Maurier's story; its 'cast' would come from a bird enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviary is a large enclosure housing birds, the 'actors' needed for The Birds.

clue.text: Where film is used for Sartre play

definitions.meaning: inside a photographic apparatus, where film is loaded
the English title of Huis Clos

explanation.surface: A location where film is used for staging a play by Sartre.
explanation.definitionFit: Film sits inside the photographic box; In Camera, meaning in private, translates Sartre's Huis Clos.

clue.text: "Our souls have trod awry in all men's sight, We'll em, till they go upright" (Fletcher, Love's Cure)

definitions.text: "Our souls have trod awry in all men's sight, We'll em, till they go upright" (Fletcher, Love's Cure)

parts.words: Our souls have trod awry in all men's sight, We'll em, till they go upright
parts.note: lines from Fletcher's play with the verb before 'em left out: what is done to prop something crooked

explanation.surface: A couplet from John Fletcher's Love's Cure with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap: to underlay is to prop up or support from beneath, so the speakers will shore up their souls until they stand straight.
explanation.definitionFit: To underlay is to support something from below, as a wedge sets a leaning object straight.

clue.text: According to Masefield's bosun, she was a casual tramp

definitions.text: According to Masefield's bosun, she was a casual tramp

parts.words: According to Masefield's bosun, she was a casual tramp
parts.note: a ship's name from John Masefield's sea verse; a tramp is a cargo steamer with no fixed route

explanation.surface: A sailor in a Masefield poem describes a woman as loose in her habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tramp' means a tramp steamer, a freighter sailing wherever cargo takes it, not a vagrant; 'she' is the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Esmeralda is the vessel named in John Masefield's sea verse, described by its bosun.

clue.text: One placed in a position of responsibility by M. G. Lewis and R.S. Thomas

definitions.text: One placed in a position of responsibility
definitions.meaning: a government official or clergyman put in charge

definitions.text: M. G. Lewis and R.S. Thomas
definitions.meaning: both writers used this word as a title

explanation.surface: A person given authority by two writers, the Gothic novelist and the Welsh poet.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabinet member or pastor holds office, and R. S. Thomas wrote a long poem titled The Minister.

clue.text: All his faces were designed to express rage or loathing (3)

definitions.text: All his faces were designed to express rage or loathing

parts.words: All his faces were designed to express rage or loathing
parts.note: Kingsley Amis's hero Jim Dixon pulls grotesque faces behind people's backs

explanation.surface: A man whose every expression was meant to show anger or disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: Jim Dixon, of Kingsley Amis's novel, makes private comic faces (his 'Edith Sitwell face' among them) to vent his loathing.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucky Jim is Kingsley Amis's 1954 comic novel, named after its face-pulling hero.

clue.text: Hilaire's sister's protagonist in rented accommodation

definitions.meaning: Marie Belloc Lowndes, sister of Hilaire Belloc, wrote a thriller about a sinister tenant
describing someone who pays to live in another's house

explanation.surface: The hero of a novel by Hilaire Belloc's sister lives in a rented room.
explanation.definitionFit: Marie Belloc Lowndes's 1913 novel The Lodger concerns a tenant; any boarder paying rent is one.

clue.text: Entertained, like Thalia, say, in commercial setting

indicators.note: setting means the advertisement surrounds the other piece like a mount round a gem

parts.note: a commercial is an advertisement, AD
Thalia is one of the nine Muses, of comedy

explanation.surface: Delighted, rather like the comic Muse appearing in an advertisement.
explanation.walkthrough: Thalia is the Muse of comedy, so 'like Thalia, say' is a Muse; 'setting' wraps the advertisement round it, and 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being amused means being entertained or made to smile.

clue.text: Merit, perhaps — severed, like A Head of Murdoch

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters given might be arranged differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A deserved place, like Iris Murdoch's novel A Severed Head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges SEVERED; 'like A Head of Murdoch' completes the picture, Iris Murdoch's novel A Severed Head.
explanation.definitionFit: To deserve something is to be worthy of it, to earn it.

clue.text: Homely, like King's animal

explanation.surface: Cosy, like a pet kept by a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Household matters are homely, and Francis King titled a novel The Domestic Animal, a tame creature.

clue.text: Some alchemist's alembic, or crucible, recalls this Massachusetts town

indicators.note: Some says just part of the letters of alchemist's alembic gives the answer

explanation.surface: A chemist's apparatus, or a melting pot, brings a New England town to mind.
explanation.walkthrough: The town spans 'alchemist's' and 'alembic'. 'crucible' recalls Arthur Miller's The Crucible, set during the Salem witch trials.
explanation.definitionFit: The Massachusetts port famous for its 1692 witch trials, setting of Miller's The Crucible.

clue.text: He is intoxicated with Liszt

parts.note: Cockney rhyming slang pairs two composers to mean drunk

explanation.surface: Someone captivated by the music of Franz Liszt.
explanation.walkthrough: In British rhyming slang 'Brahms and Liszt' means drunk (rhyming with an impolite word for it), so the other composer 'with Liszt' is intoxicated.
explanation.definitionFit: Johannes Brahms is joined to Liszt in the rhyming-slang phrase for being drunk.

clue.text: Located at Uncle's by Fergus Hume

definitions.text: Located at Uncle's by Fergus Hume

parts.words: Located at Uncle's by Fergus Hume
parts.note: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker; Hume wrote of a heroine of the pawn-shop

explanation.surface: Someone found staying at a relative's house in a Fergus Hume story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle's' is old British slang for a pawnshop; Fergus Hume's novel is Hagar of the Pawn-Shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Hagar is the gypsy heroine of Fergus Hume's Hagar of the Pawn-Shop.

clue.text: Prospero's was identified on Corfu by Durrell

definitions.text: Prospero's was identified on Corfu by Durrell

parts.words: Prospero's was identified on Corfu by Durrell
parts.note: Lawrence Durrell's Corfu memoir names the island as the magician's home from The Tempest

explanation.surface: A writer claims to have found the magician's dwelling on a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Tempest Prospero lives in a cave-like dwelling; Lawrence Durrell's Corfu book is Prospero's Cell.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero's small dwelling in The Tempest is so called, as in Durrell's title Prospero's Cell.

clue.text: Some finer Rolls-Royce for Fauntleroy

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A grander luxury car bought for the young lord of the novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Lord Fauntleroy's own name is Cedric Errol, so 'for Fauntleroy' points to his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Cedric Errol is the American boy who becomes Lord Fauntleroy in Frances Hodgson Burnett's story.

clue.text: Paul Tillich presented his view of culture

definitions.text: Paul Tillich presented his view of culture

parts.words: Paul Tillich presented his view of culture
parts.note: Tillich wrote Theology of Culture, so he is one who studies divinity

explanation.surface: A thinker set out his opinions on culture.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Tillich, the German-American Protestant thinker, wrote Theology of Culture, so he was such a student of God.
explanation.definitionFit: A theologer is an old word for a scholar of religion, as Tillich was.
